top_level_objectives: Identify the major structural features of the DNA double helix, including the sugar-phosphate backbone, complementary base pairing, and antiparallel strand orientation.
Explain how DNA polymerase, helicase, single-strand binding proteins, and DNA ligase coordinate DNA replication.
Describe why leading- and lagging-strand synthesis differ and how these differences arise from DNA’s antiparallel structure.
Interpret semiconservative replication as the production of daughter DNA molecules containing one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the overall three-dimensional form of DNA and orient students to the molecule they will be examining.
key_visuals: A smooth rotating double helix suspended in space
Visible outer sugar-phosphate backbones spiraling around a central axis
Base pairs projecting inward like rungs of a twisted ladder
student_actions: Rotate and inspect the helix from different angles.
Identify the double-helix shape as the structural basis for DNA.

scenes.brief_purpose: Break the helix into its main chemical parts and reinforce which bases pair with each other.
key_visuals: Color-coded bases labeled adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine
Hydrogen-bond connections between A–T and G–C
Backbone segments framing the paired bases
student_actions: Select individual bases to see their names and pairings.
Compare the two bond types and note that G–C is stabilized by three hydrogen bonds while A–T has two.

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how strand directionality creates the antiparallel arrangement of DNA.
key_visuals: 5' and 3' labels at opposite ends of each strand
Arrows along the two backbones pointing in opposite directions
A close-up view emphasizing the offset, antiparallel alignment
student_actions: Trace each strand from one end to the other.
Determine which strand runs 5' to 3' and which runs 3' to 5'.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the start of replication and the enzymes that prepare DNA for copying.
key_visuals: A replication fork opening as the helix unwinds
Helicase positioned at the fork separating the strands
Single-strand binding proteins coating the exposed DNA
student_actions: Observe how the double helix is unwound.
Identify the role of helicase and explain how binding proteins keep the strands separated.

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how DNA polymerase synthesizes new strands and why synthesis differs on the two templates.
key_visuals: DNA polymerase moving along template strands
Continuous extension on the leading strand
Short Okazaki fragments forming on the lagging strand
student_actions: Watch polymerase add nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction.
Compare leading- and lagging-strand synthesis and connect the difference to antiparallel template orientation.

scenes.brief_purpose: Conclude with strand joining and the meaning of semiconservative replication.
key_visuals: DNA ligase sealing gaps between Okazaki fragments
Each daughter molecule showing one old strand and one new strand
student_actions: Identify where ligase acts to complete the lagging strand.
Verify that each daughter DNA molecule contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand, and state why replication is semiconservative.
